To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
CRFR1 antagonists in BLA can attenuate fear conditioned decreases in sleep, but do not alter conditioned fear behavior or fear induced temperature increases.

CRFR1 antagonists in BLA can attenuate conditioned fear‐related changes in sleep, but not freezing or stress‐related hyperthermia, and that these effects depend on the rats’ vulnerability to fear conditioning.
post-training CRFR1 antagonization in BLA blocks shock-induced decreases in REM sleep in resilient rats and attenuates the extinction of shock-induced increases in REM sleep in vulnerable rats.
In summary, our research is concerned with

understanding the neural mechanisms that underlie individual differences in the behavioral and physiological responses to stress and the role of the brain in the development and treatment of psychiatric disorders.
the role of the amygdaloid complex in the modulation of sleep and the relationship between sleep and stress responses.
the neurobiology of individual differences in fear memory and stress.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
CRF in BLA plays an important role in mediating the fear‐induced decrease in REM sleep in vulnerable rats.
CRFR1 antagonists may be a potential target to increase sleep in individuals suffering from insomnia and anxiety disorders, but that this needs to be further investigated.

CRFR1 antagonists in BLA can attenuate fear conditioning‐induced changes in REM sleep, but only in vulnerable rats, and not in resilient rats, and that this is not related to fear‐conditioned freezing behavior or SIH, but is related to the fear‐conditioning induced reduction in REM sleep on CTX1.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the CRFR1 antagonist blocks the fear conditioning‐induced decrease in REM in vulnerable but not resilient rats and that this effect is not associated with changes in freezing or stress‐induced hyperthemia.

the CRFR1 antagonist in BLA blocks the fear conditioned decrease in REM sleep in rats that show this response to fear conditioning, but does not alter the fear conditioned decrease or increase in REM in rats that show no change or an increase in REM following fear conditioning.
CRF in the BLA is involved in the expression of fear‐conditioned changes in sleep and that CRFR1 antagonists can be used to block these effects.
The main takeaway from our work is that
CRFR1 antagonists may be useful in promoting REM sleep and REM sleep dependent learning.
CRFR1 in the basolatera amygdala plays a significant role on the effects of fear conditioning on sleep and that CRFR1 antagonists may be effective in the treatment of PTSD.
CRFR1 in the amygdala can be a target for treatment for sleep disturbances that are associated with fear conditioning.
